title: Faion corpus variable dictionary
description: The one place a template variable is defined. A template's <name>.vars.schema.json $refs into #/$defs/<var> and adds only what is genuinely local. Measured from all 2,919 Markdown templates under skills/faion/knowledge/*/*/templates/ via tpl-migrate.py: 14,959 placeholder candidates, 7,833 of them nameable.
$comment: RULE OF ENTRY (template-jinja-migration.md §3): an entry is a name PLUS a meaning. Two uses share a name only when a value carried from one artefact to another through <project>/.faion/template-params.json is still correct. Convergence therefore produces MORE names, not fewer — `name` at 676 occurrences is the worst variable in the corpus because it means 676 things, and it is deliberately absent from this file. Every entry whose $comment names an alternative meaning was split on purpose; re-merging it is a regression, not a cleanup. `$defs` is used per the convention; under draft-07 it is an unknown keyword and $ref resolves against it by plain JSON pointer.

artefact_id.title: Artefact ID
artefact_id.description: What unique id names this artefact? The corpus convention is <artefact-slug>-<client-slug>-<YYYY-MM-DD>, e.g. growth-webinar-delivery-acme-2026-08-16.
artefact_id.$comment: NOT merged with artefact_slug. artefact_id is the whole composite string; artefact_slug is one component of it. The renderer has no expressions (§2.3 keeps that ban), so nothing can derive one from the other and both must be asked for. Measured: 74 templates write `artefact_id`: <slug>-<client>-<YYYY-MM-DD>, 117 more write the same slot HTML-escaped as <artefact_id>, 6 write it as a table cell.

artefact_slug.title: Artefact slug
artefact_slug.description: What kebab-case slug names this artefact — lowercase words joined by hyphens, no spaces? Usually the methodology slug the template came from.
artefact_slug.$comment: NOT merged with artefact_id (composite, see there) and NOT merged with client_slug (a different party). The corpus writes this as <slug>, <kebab-case slug> and <kebab-case-slug> in 58+ templates; all three are one variable.

artefact_title.title: Title
artefact_title.description: What title should appear as the document's H1?
artefact_title.$comment: NOT merged with artefact_slug: a title is prose for a reader ('Q3 Webinar Delivery Runbook'), a slug is an identifier. Templates that render `# <Title> — <artefact_id>` need both in one line.

artefact_date.title: Artefact date
artefact_date.description: What date is this artefact produced on, as YYYY-MM-DD?
artefact_date.$comment: Split from last_reviewed_date, start_date, end_date and due_date. `date` was proposed 267 times across 10 domains and covered all five meanings; carrying a review date into a produced-on field is exactly the silent wrong value the dictionary exists to stop.

document_version.title: Version
document_version.description: What semantic version is this revision of the document — bumped on every refresh?
document_version.$comment: The corpus spells this <semver> (28 uses) and <version>; both are the DOCUMENT's version. NOT the version of the software the document is about — a template needing that declares a local `subject_version`.

document_status.title: Status
document_status.description: What lifecycle state is this document in right now?
document_status.$comment: NOT merged with rag_status or pass_fail. This is the state of the DOCUMENT; those two are judgements about the thing the document reports on.

last_reviewed_date.title: Last reviewed
last_reviewed_date.description: When was this document last reviewed by a human, as YYYY-MM-DD?
last_reviewed_date.$comment: 919 templates carry a last_reviewed line; the corpus spells the slot <ISO-date>, <ISO date>, <iso date> and YYYY-MM-DD. Split from artefact_date: a document produced in May and reviewed in August has two different correct answers.

next_review_date.title: Next review
next_review_date.description: By when must this document be reviewed again, as YYYY-MM-DD?
next_review_date.$comment: Split from due_date. A review date is a maintenance obligation on the document; a due date is a delivery obligation on the work. Merging them makes an overdue task look like a stale doc.

review_cadence.title: Review cadence
review_cadence.description: How often is this document reviewed?
review_cadence.$comment: Vocabulary widened past the corpus's `monthly | quarterly` because 'weekly' and 'ad-hoc' both appear in prose beside the slot. An enum too narrow to say the true answer is worse than a string.

owner_full_name.title: Owner (full name)
owner_full_name.description: Who is accountable for this artefact — one named human, full name? Never a team or a group.
owner_full_name.$comment: 814 templates carry an owner slot in roughly 30 spellings — <Full Name> <email>, <@handle>, <named-human>, <single-named-handle>, role:<handle>, <role>:<person>, <name @handle>, <handle or email — single named human, never "team">. All name the same person, so they converge here, on owner_email, owner_handle and owner_role. Split from author_name, reviewer_name, sponsor_name and next_action_owner: on a design doc the author wrote it, the owner maintains it, the reviewer signed it and the sponsor paid for it, and carrying any one into another is wrong more often than right. Sensitive per template-builder.md §5a — an identified person.

owner_email.title: Owner email
owner_email.description: What email address reaches the owner?
owner_email.$comment: Kept apart from owner_full_name because 71 templates render `owner: <Full Name> <email>` — one line, two slots — and 59 more render a single slot that accepts either. A template that wants the either-form $refs owner_handle.

owner_handle.title: Owner handle
owner_handle.description: What chat or repo handle identifies the owner (e.g. @tetiana)?
owner_handle.$comment: 189 templates use <@handle> as the owner slot. Sensitive for the same reason as the name: a handle identifies a person, and template-builder.md §5a puts personal data on the same footing as a credential.

owner_role.title: Owner role
owner_role.description: What role does the owner hold in this engagement (e.g. tech-lead, PM, BA)?
owner_role.$comment: The role half of `owner: <role>:<person>` (11 templates) and `owner: role:<handle>` (19). NOT sensitive — a role names a seat, not a person. Emphatically NOT merged with user_role: this is who maintains the document, user_role is the actor in a user story.

reviewer_name.title: Reviewer
reviewer_name.description: Who reviews and signs this artefact off? One named human.
reviewer_name.$comment: 55 templates carry the `## Sign-off` envelope `- reviewer: <name>` / `- approved: <yes / no>` alongside `- owner: <name>`, in the same file — proof inside one artefact that reviewer and owner are two people. The approver is deliberately merged INTO this entry: in that envelope the reviewer is the one who sets `approved`, so a separate approver_name would have no distinct value to carry.

author_name.title: Author
author_name.$comment: Split from owner_full_name. Authorship is a fact fixed at writing time; ownership moves. sdd/design-docs-patterns renders `**Author:** [Name]` on a document whose owner line names someone else.

sponsor_name.title: Sponsor
sponsor_name.description: Who sponsors this work — the person who funds it and can override a red status?
sponsor_name.$comment: Split from owner_full_name on the strongest evidence in the corpus: pm/benefits-realization-pm-traditional/realization-report.md heads a block 'Sponsor Override (if softening RED)'. A document whose sponsor and owner are the same person cannot have an override.

session_facilitator.title: Facilitator
session_facilitator.description: Who runs this session — the facilitator, moderator or interviewer?
session_facilitator.$comment: Interviewer and moderator are merged in on purpose: across ba/remote-workshop-toolkit, ux/usability-testing and research interview guides the slot asks the same question — who is in the room running it — and a value carried between them stays correct. Split from owner_full_name, which on a session guide is whoever maintains the guide, not whoever runs the session.

candidate_name.title: Candidate name
candidate_name.description: Which candidate does this record evaluate? Full name.
candidate_name.$comment: The ratified first use of `sensitive` for personal rather than credential data (template-builder.md §5a, hr/structured-interview-design/templates/scorecard.md). Split from participant_code: a hiring record names an identified person and must never reach the multi-tenant assembler, a research pseudonym exists precisely so that it can.

participant_code.title: Participant code
participant_code.description: What anonymised code identifies this research participant (e.g. P01)?
participant_code.$comment: Deliberately NOT sensitive, and deliberately NOT merged with candidate_name or any real name. ux and research templates write `# Interview Notes — Participant [ID]` and attribute quotes as 'P01, Day 3'. Declaring this sensitive would defeat the pseudonym; putting a real name in it would defeat the study's ethics approval, which is why the question says code.

next_action_owner.title: Next-action owner
next_action_owner.description: Who owns the next action coming out of this artefact?
next_action_owner.$comment: Split from owner_full_name on 22 templates that render `- <YYYY-MM-DD> — <owner> — <next-action>` and 17 that render `- [owner] — [imperative sentence] — [date]` inside documents whose header already names a different owner. This is the clearest instance of §3's test: the value carried from the header to the action line is wrong.

client_name.title: Client name
client_name.description: Which client is this engagement for — the name as it should appear to a reader?
client_name.$comment: NOT marked sensitive. §5a's test is 'would this value identify a person, or open a door'; an organisation is neither, and marking it sensitive would keep the assembler from rendering the one word most of these documents are addressed to. A template for a sole trader whose client IS a named person declares a local sensitive variable instead.

client_slug.title: Client slug
client_slug.description: What short kebab-case token stands for the client inside identifiers (e.g. acme)?
client_slug.$comment: Split from client_name because artefact_id concatenates it into a filename-safe string while headings render the display name. 64 templates use the <client> slot in artefact_id; a further 15 use <context> in the same position, which is the SAME variable spelled differently — those converge here only when the value really is the client. Where <context> means a workstream rather than a client, the template declares a local variable.

engagement_name.title: Engagement
engagement_name.description: Which engagement does this artefact belong to?
engagement_name.$comment: 55 ba templates open with `- engagement: <name>`. Split from both client_name and project_name: one client can run three engagements, and an engagement can cover several projects. tpl-migrate named this slot `name`, which is how 55 files would have inherited the corpus's worst variable.

project_name.title: Project name
project_name.$comment: Split from product_name and engagement_name. pm renders `# Cost Estimate — [Project Name]` on work that may or may not have a product attached; §3 names product_name/project_name/team_name as exactly the collapse not to make.

product_name.title: Product name
product_name.description: What is the product called — the name a customer would recognise?
product_name.$comment: Split from project_name and company_name. marketing renders it inside customer-facing copy ('Welcome to [Product]!'), where the project codename would be wrong and the company name would be wrong differently.

company_name.title: Our company name
company_name.description: What is the name of the company sending or producing this — ours, not the client's?
company_name.$comment: Split from client_name, and the split matters because both appear in one document: marketing/growth-affiliate-marketing renders 'Welcome to the [Company] Affiliate Program' in a letter addressed to a client. Merging them puts the recipient's name on the sender's line.

team_name.title: Team name
team_name.$comment: Named in §3 as a collapse not to make. Kept even though it is only 8 occurrences, because the collapse it prevents (into `name`) is the one the whole dictionary is for.

feature_name.title: Feature name
feature_name.description: Which feature does this artefact cover?
feature_name.$comment: Split from product_name. sdd renders `# Implementation Plan: [Feature Name]` and `# Design: [Feature Name]` inside a repo whose product name is fixed; carrying the product name in would name every plan the same thing.

repo_name.title: Repository
repo_name.description: Which repository does this refer to (owner/name, or the bare name if unambiguous)?
repo_name.$comment: The <repo> in `git://<repo>/<path>` and the <name> in `~/workspace/repos/<name>`. Split from project_name: a project routinely spans several repos, which is why the corpus writes both slots on the same line in ai-core/prompt-portability-audit.

source_url.title: Source URL
source_url.description: What URL is this claim or figure taken from?
source_url.$comment: Split from evidence_root and trigger_url. `url` (111) and `link` (41) are one meaning in two spellings and converge here; the two entries below are different questions that also happened to be spelled <URL>.

source_captured_date.title: Captured on
source_captured_date.description: On what date was this source captured, as YYYY-MM-DD? A URL without a capture date is not a citation.
source_captured_date.$comment: The corpus writes `[URL, captured YYYY-MM-DD]`, `<url + date>` and `| [URL] | YYYY-MM-DD |` in competitor and trend reports. Split from artefact_date: a report written today can cite a page captured last quarter, and merging them silently backdates or forward-dates every citation.

evidence_root.title: Evidence root
evidence_root.description: Where does the evidence for this artefact live — one link a reader can open to find all of it?
evidence_root.$comment: 12 skeleton templates carry `evidence_root: <link>` in frontmatter beside per-claim source URLs. Split from source_url: one is a directory, the others are leaves, and a value carried either way points a reader at the wrong level.

evidence_source_ref.title: Evidence reference
evidence_source_ref.description: What identifies the evidence behind this claim — a URL, a transcript id, a ticket key or a dashboard name?
evidence_source_ref.$comment: 209 templates carry `<source path or URL>` or `<URL / transcript_id / ticket / dashboard>`. Split from source_url and given type string rather than format uri precisely because a transcript id and a ticket key are legitimate answers and a uri format would reject them.

evidence_quote.title: Verbatim quote
evidence_quote.description: What did the source actually say, word for word? Paraphrase belongs elsewhere.
evidence_quote.$comment: NOT marked sensitive, because the corpus attributes quotes to participant_code rather than to names. A template that attributes a quote to an identified person must declare its attribution slot sensitive; the quote text alone does not carry the identity.

trigger_url.title: Trigger URL
trigger_url.description: What URL points at the thing that triggered this artefact — the alert, the PR, the ticket?
trigger_url.$comment: Split from source_url. In 19 dev and infra skeletons `trigger_url` sits in frontmatter and `- <URL 1>` sits under `# Evidence` in the same file: one says why the document exists, the others say why its claims are true.

trigger_kind.title: Trigger kind
trigger_kind.description: What kind of thing triggered this artefact — a discrete event, a threshold being crossed, or a schedule firing?
trigger_kind.$comment: Verbatim from 19 templates writing `- kind: <event | threshold | schedule>`. Closed because the corpus closed it, not because three felt like enough.

decision_statement.title: Decision
decision_statement.description: What was decided? One declarative sentence naming the choice, not the deliberation.
decision_statement.$comment: The `<single declarative sentence>` and `<decision text — one of the enumerated outcomes>` slots. Split from decision_rationale, which the same templates place in the next section — the corpus is explicit that the verdict and the reasons are two fields.

decision_rationale.title: Rationale
decision_rationale.description: Why was that decided? Two or more sentences citing at least one named input.
decision_rationale.$comment: `<≥2 sentences; cite at least one input by name>`. Composed rather than typed: this is the old `text` type from template-builder.md §3 — the agent writes it from the author's answer.

scope_summary.title: Scope
scope_summary.description: What is in scope here? One paragraph.

out_of_scope.title: Out of scope
out_of_scope.description: What is explicitly NOT covered, that a reader might otherwise assume is?
out_of_scope.$comment: Typed array rather than a numbered family. The corpus writes `- [exclusion]` repeated under `## Out of Scope`; per-line placeholders cannot be variables (§2.3 has no loops), but the section as a whole is one answer.

open_questions.title: Open questions
open_questions.description: What is still unresolved that a reviewer needs to know about?
open_questions.$comment: Same shape as out_of_scope, and the same reason: the corpus's `- [Question 2]` / `<question pending review>` rows are not 2, 3 and 4 distinct variables.

notes.title: Notes
notes.description: Anything else a reader needs — follow-up actions, downstream owners, review schedule? Leave empty if there is nothing.
notes.$comment: The `<optional>` and `<optional follow-up actions, downstream owners, review schedule>` slot in 59 templates. Carries a default of empty string on purpose: an optional section that refuses by name when unanswered would block every build.

approved.title: Approved
approved.description: Has the reviewer approved this artefact?
approved.$comment: Boolean, not the corpus's `<yes / no>` string (73 occurrences in 55 templates). The renderer decides how to spell it; a schema that stores 'yes' invites 'Y', 'yes ', 'approved' and 'signed' into the same field.

severity.title: Severity
severity.description: How bad is this finding if nothing is done about it?
severity.$comment: Split from priority and from confidence_level, all three of which the corpus spells with the same three words. Severity is about the harm, priority is about the order of work, confidence is about how sure we are — three questions, three answers, and merging them makes a low-confidence finding look harmless.

priority.title: Priority
priority.description: How urgently should this be worked on relative to everything else?
priority.$comment: Four values, not severity's three, because the corpus writes `Critical / High / Medium / Low` for priority and `[low, medium, high]` for severity. MoSCoW (must/should/could/won't) is deliberately NOT folded in: it appears 3 times, it is a commitment vocabulary rather than an urgency one, and a template that needs it declares it locally.

rag_status.title: RAG status
rag_status.description: Is this on track, at risk, or off track?
rag_status.$comment: Split from pass_fail and document_status. A red item still exists and is still being worked; a failed check is finished and negative. 34 pm templates write `green / amber / red` in the same tables that carry pass/fail elsewhere.

pass_fail.title: Result
pass_fail.description: Did this check meet its bar?
pass_fail.$comment: The corpus's `[Hit/Miss]` (11 marketing occurrences) is merged in on purpose: 'did the metric hit its target' and 'did the diagnostic pass' are the same question about different subjects, and a value carried between them stays correct. `PASS/FAIL` uppercase is the same variable.

confidence_level.title: Confidence
confidence_level.description: How confident are you in this figure or claim?
confidence_level.$comment: Spelled `[High/Med/Low]` in 66 research and market-sizing rows. Split from severity — see there. Not merged with a percentage confidence interval, which is a number and belongs in a local variable.

metric_name.title: Metric
metric_name.description: Which metric is being tracked — named precisely enough that someone else could pull the same number?
metric_name.$comment: Split from measurement_method: the metric is what is counted, the method is where the count comes from. The corpus writes them as adjacent columns.

metric_baseline.title: Baseline
metric_baseline.description: What is the metric's value today, before this work?
metric_baseline.$comment: The `[current]` and `[baseline]` columns. Split from metric_target — a table row carrying the target into the baseline column reports success on day zero. Typed string, not integer, because the corpus writes '$4.2k', '62%' and '3.1s' in this slot.

metric_target.title: Target
metric_target.description: What value would count as success, and by when?
metric_target.$comment: NOT merged with target_audience, which the corpus also spells `[target]`, and NOT merged with the migration sense of `[Target]` ('Migrate from [Source] to [Target]') — that one is a system_name.

measurement_method.title: How measured
measurement_method.description: How is this measured — which query, dashboard or tool produces the number?
measurement_method.$comment: Absorbs the corpus's `[How]`, `[method]` and `[tool]` columns where they sit beside a metric. `[Tool]` in a cost worksheet is a purchased product, not this — that is a product_name.

sample_size.title: Sample size
sample_size.description: How many participants, sessions or observations does this rest on?
sample_size.$comment: The `[N]`, `[n]` and `[N participants]` slots where they mean a count. tpl-migrate refuses these as format tokens (154 occurrences) because [N] alone carries no meaning; only the ones whose label says participants, sessions or observations belong here.

start_date.title: Start date
start_date.description: When does this start, as YYYY-MM-DD?

end_date.title: End date
end_date.description: When does this end, as YYYY-MM-DD?
end_date.$comment: Split from due_date. `**Timeline:** [Start date] — [End date]` describes a window that has already been agreed; a due date is a commitment that can be missed.

due_date.title: Due date
due_date.description: By when must this be done, as YYYY-MM-DD?
due_date.$comment: Split from next_review_date and end_date — see both.

period_label.title: Period
period_label.description: Which reporting period does this cover (e.g. 2026-Q3, 2026-W33, August 2026)?
period_label.$comment: The corpus writes <YYYY-Www>, Q[X] [Year] and [Month]. One variable, because every spelling answers 'which period'. Split from start_date/end_date: a label is what a reader recognises, a date pair is what a query filters on.

target_audience.title: Target audience
target_audience.description: Who is this for — the audience, described specifically enough to exclude someone?
target_audience.$comment: The `[Who]` beside a 'Target audience' label. Split from persona_name and user_role: an audience is a segment, a persona is a named archetype, a user_role is the actor in one story.

persona_name.title: Persona
persona_name.description: Which named persona is this about (e.g. 'Ops Olena')?
persona_name.$comment: Split from user_role although the corpus uses <persona> in both `As a <persona>` and `**Persona:** [Persona]`. A persona is a research artefact with a name and a document behind it; a user_role is a job title in a sentence. ba/requirements-documentation renders `As a <persona>`, ux/journey-mapping renders `**Persona:** [Persona]`, and carrying 'admin' into the second is as wrong as carrying 'Ops Olena' into the first.

user_role.title: User role
user_role.description: In this user story, what role is the actor in — 'As a ___'?
user_role.$comment: Emphatically split from owner_role. Both are spelled <role> and both mean 'a job title', but one is who maintains the document and the other is who uses the software. 65 occurrences of `role` across 8 domains sat on this fault line.

user_capability.title: Capability wanted
user_capability.description: What does the user want to be able to do — 'I want ___'?

user_benefit.title: Benefit
user_benefit.description: Why does the user want it — 'so that ___'? State an observable outcome, not a restatement of the capability.
user_benefit.$comment: The corpus writes this slot as <value> in ba and [benefit] in pm/gitlab-boards. Merged, because both ask 'so that what'. NOT merged with the ai-agents <value> slot, which is a config value — see the findings note on `value`.

channel_name.title: Channel
channel_name.description: Which channel is this about — the route to the audience (e.g. paid search, newsletter, partner referral)?
channel_name.$comment: Split from platform_name. A channel is a strategy ('paid social'), a platform is a product you log into ('Meta Ads Manager'). marketing templates put them in adjacent columns of one table.

system_name.title: System
system_name.description: Which named system is this — the one a reader could find in a service catalogue?
system_name.$comment: The corpus is explicit in ba/business-process-analysis: the column header reads '[Named system only]'. Split from platform_name and product_name; also the correct home for the `[Target]` in 'Migrate from [Source] to [Target]'.

platform_name.title: Platform
platform_name.description: Which platform or vendor product is this on?
platform_name.$comment: Split from channel_name — see there — and from system_name, which is something we run rather than something we buy.

file_path.title: Path
file_path.description: What repository-relative path does this refer to?
file_path.$comment: Split from source_url and evidence_source_ref. A path is resolved against a repo, not fetched; sdd/sdd-workflow-overview renders `- CREATE: \`[path/to/new-file.ext]\` — [purpose]`, where a URL would be meaningless.
